pages.text: Skipper squawked through his megaphone at the harbor dock. Pip held up a puffy sea-sponge cake baked just right. Skipper's orders sent the sweet treat on a tiny rowboat across the bay.

The cake came back from the distant island completely flat! The island kitchen had cold salty winds and no warm oven. Building a whole heavy little ship for one tiny pastry had taken too long, and the recipe ruined.

Pip flipped open his Instruction Booklet to see what went wrong. Wally swam alongside the harbor pier with a gentle splash. Pip realized the cake needed its own exact air, bowl, and warmth packed alongside it.

Pip packed the fresh batter, a pinch of warm salt, and his favorite spoon into a wooden sea-chest. The Instruction Booklet made this sealed crate a finished model of everything the cake needed. Wally did the work, strapping the light crate onto his back instead of towing a heavy ship.

Wally sped across the water and returned with the open sea-chest. Inside, the cake stayed perfectly tall and warm, exactly like it was at home! A tiny friendly light flickered on across the faraway horizon dock.

Skipper squawked a loud cheer through his megaphone. But Pip looked down at the dock and saw three different friends asking for three different deliveries. How could one Instruction Booklet build crates for all of them?

High on the lighthouse deck, Skipper ruffled his feathers. Down below, packed crates waited across the harbor, but someone needed to direct the lifting. Pip opened the harbor logbook to help keep track.

Skipper squawked loud instructions through his megaphone into the quiet morning mist. Nothing moved on the water, and no crates were lifted. Skipper was shouting his orders across the wrong bay, where nobody was listening.

Pip tugged the brass megaphone around so it faced the harbor channel instead. 'Skipper's orders must reach the one who does the heavy lifting,' Pip explained. 'You call out the plan, and the water channel carries your words straight to the worker.'

Skipper blew a sharp squawk through the megaphone: 'Build the stack, run the line, secure the crate!' Down in the water, Wally heard every clear word. Wally's work began immediately as he caught the crate on his back.

Skipper gave another order from his high perch, and Wally gently set a finished model of a toy lighthouse into the crate. Skipper never had to touch the heavy wood himself. Wally did all the heavy lifting because the agreed signal channel connected them perfectly.

Wally glided out, and a second delivery light sparkled on the distant horizon. Skipper beamed, tapping his megaphone proudly. But down on the main dock, an enormous pile of mixed cargo sat waiting, with no plan for what should go inside the next crate.
Skipper squawked through his megaphone from his wooden post. Wally listened and did all of Wally's work out in the deep water. Two friendly lights twinkled back from the distant island.
Then Skipper wanted to give orders over on the dry shore. When Skipper shouted, Wally could not move across the dry sand. Whales need deep water to swim and carry big loads.
Pip ran across the beach with an idea. Pip set up a special rolling water tank that holds ocean water anywhere on land. Now Wally could have his own swimming pool right on dry ground.
Both pieces were set up together so the work could begin. Wally slid right into the floating tank and floated easily on the sand. Skipper's orders could finally reach Wally even away from the sea.
Pip brought out a tiny starter crate to test the new setup. Wally balanced the cheerful little box right on his head without any trouble. It worked, sending a cheerful greeting to everyone on shore.

Out on the horizon, a third bright light popped on. But Pip noticed the little crate was very plain and needed some color. How were they going to build lots of identical crates with proper tools inside?
Pip wanted to fix the island docks. Long ago, the harbor built a whole new giant wagon just to hold one little wrench. The huge wagon was too slow to roll across the sand!
Skipper squawked through his horn. 'Do not build a whole heavy wagon!' he shouted. 'A container wraps only your job and its exact tools inside one light box.'
Pip found a plain standard crate. He tucked in his dock plan, his favorite hammer, and a coil of sturdy rope. With every needed piece packed tightly together, he shut the lid tight.

Wally floated near the shore with his water tank ready. Pip slid the neat wooden box onto Wally's back. Because the box carried everything inside, Pip's dock chore worked the exact same way on the dry pier as it did on the sand.
Pip wanted to run a small clock in the packing shed. In the old days, every app needed a whole giant computer called a virtual machine. The heavy iron cart was far too slow to push along the dock.

Pip decided to pack a container instead. He placed just the little clock and the two exact gears it needed inside a neat, plain crate. A container wraps only the app and its parts, with no extra junk.
Skipper squawked through his megaphone from his post. He tapped the tight lid with his wing. The crate was sealed tight so the parts inside could never change.

Wally rested the light crate on his back with a gentle splash. Because everything was packed inside, the clock ticked identically on this dock or across the wide ocean. It did not need a whole heavy machine to run.

Pip wanted to share his berry-baking machine with the outer harbor. In the past, he had to build a giant wooden house just to hold one tiny pan. The whole house was far too heavy, and moving it took forever!
Wally nudged a neat, lightweight crate forward with his nose. 'A container does not need a whole heavy house,' Wally said. 'You only pack the recipe and the exact tools it needs to cook.'

Pip packed the batter and spoon into the snug crate and closed the lid. Since each box rested easily on the very same dock, Pip could stack three boxes without tiring out. They did not drag along extra walls or heavy floors anymore.

Skipper squawked through his megaphone from his wooden post. 'A container wraps one job with its own parts, so it works anywhere you put it!' Pip smiled as the crate sat neatly on the boards, running smooth and fast.

Pip wanted to build a clock on the dock. In the old way, he had to drag an entire heavy shed and giant iron wheels just to run one tiny tick-tock. The heavy machinery was slow and took up too much room.

Wally swam up with a clever idea. Instead of building a whole heavy machine, they could use a container! A container wraps just one program together with the exact tools it needs inside a single sealed box.

Pip placed the clockwork gears and a winding key inside the neat wooden crate. Because everything was enclosed together, no parts could get lost. The container held every tool needed to run, completely separate from the rest of the dock.

Skipper carried the box over to a jagged rock across the harbor. When he opened the latch, the little clockwork gears turned just as smoothly as they had on the dock boards. A container runs the exact same way on any island you bring it to!

title: Pip and the Special Wooden Crates

pages.text: Pip stared at the docks where a mountain of heavy wooden sheds sat waiting to move. Each giant shed carried an entire workshop just to hold a single pair of pliers. This old way was far too slow and heavy to carry anywhere.
Wally nudged a neat, small crate onto the dock with his nose. A container is like this little box, he explained. We pack just the tool and its exact parts inside without the giant house.

Pip placed a hammer inside the box along with the exact nails it needed, then fastened the lid tight. Because everything was sealed inside together, the hammer could do its job anywhere. It did not need the harbor workshop to work properly.
Skipper squawked through his megaphone from his wooden post. The crate sits the same on rocky beaches, sandy shores, and wooden piers! It runs anywhere without building a whole new island first.
Wally wanted to share his favorite game with Pip. He knew Pip loved playing too.
Pip asked Wally, 'How do I play your game, Wally?'
Wally decided to pack the game with all its parts. He wanted Pip to play just like he did.
Pip watched as Wally carefully packed the game. Everything was neatly placed inside.
Pip wanted to share his favorite game on the village dock. Long ago, people dragged a giant heavy wooden table everywhere just to hold one toy. It was much too slow, and it made Pip's paws ache.
Skipper squawked through his horn from his post. He told Pip that a container is like a neat lunchbox that holds only one game and the exact tools to play it. It leaves the heavy furniture behind!
Pip gathered the wooden blocks and the rule scroll into a single tidy box. A container wraps the app with every single piece it needs to run. He latched the lid tight so nothing was missing.

Wally smiled as he carried the light box across the open sea lanes. Because everything was packed inside, the game played exactly the same way on Wally's back as it did on the shore. It did not need a whole heavy island to work!

Pip wanted to play a spinning game on the far side of the dock. In the old days, villagers built a giant stone shed with a heavy engine just to spin one tiny top. It was too slow and heavy to carry anywhere.

Pip found a better way by using a light wooden crate. A container is a sealed box that holds one game along with the exact string it needs to spin. It does not carry an entire stone shed, only the parts that make it work.

Wally swam up to inspect the box on the harbor boards. Because every single tool was sealed inside, the game spun perfectly on the wet planks just like it did on dry stone. The container makes the game run the exact same way on every dock.

Pip was delighted to see how easy it was to move the game around. Instead of dragging heavy machines, Pip could stack sealed crates and hand them to anyone. The container was ready to travel anywhere without missing a single piece.

Pip wanted to share his harbor counting game across the island. At first, he tried building a whole heavy wooden desk with drawers and wheels just to hold one tiny notebook. It was much too big to move, and the heavy frame made everything slow.

Wally swam up to the dock with a warm smile. He explained that a container is like a tiny, neat crate holding only the game and the exact pencil it needs to work. Leaving the heavy desk behind makes the box light and easy to handle.

Pip tucked the game rules and the right tools inside a small, plain crate. He tapped the lid down tight so nothing extra could get in or fall out. Because everything it needed was sealed inside, the crate would work the exact same way on any dock.

Skipper called out through his horn as Pip set the box onto a stone pillar. The lid popped open, and the counting game started up instantly without needing a whole new desk. It ran just as smoothly on the stone as it had on the wooden pier.

title: The Tale of the Standard Box

pages.text: Skipper looked down at the wooden dock with a groan. To run a simple harbor clock on the pier, the crew had hauled a huge, clunky iron machine. Building a whole giant computer just to run one tiny tool was far too heavy and slow.

Pip found a smarter way in the packing shed. He placed the clockwork gears inside one neat, plain box along with its exact little wrench. A container packs just the app and the few tools it needs to tick, leaving all the heavy junk behind.

Wally nudged the crate onto his back to test it out. A container runs identically anywhere because everything it needs is sealed inside the standard walls. When he set it down on a rocking raft, the clock chimed on the exact same second as it did on the stone dock.

Skipper squawked into his megaphone with delight. No more rebuilding gigantic engines or guessing what might break on a new pier! Every harbor station could run the exact same boxed job without changing a single nail.

Pip wanted to share his clockwork toy with the whole harbor. In the old days, sharing meant lugging an entire giant iron machine just to tick once. It was way too heavy, and the gears always jammed on the salty wooden planks.

Pip tried a smarter plan. He took a plain crate and tucked inside his toy clock along with the exact winding key and spring it needed to run. A container wraps one program with all its tools so nothing gets left behind.

Skipper landed on the stone dock to test the closed box. The sealed crate opened up and the clock started ticking right on time without changing a single gear. Because the box holds everything inside, it works the exact same way on any dock in the harbor.

Wally swam up and balanced the tidy crate on his smooth back. Instead of hauling a mountain of heavy iron, he could carry the light box anywhere with a gentle wave of his fin. The little toy ran just as smoothly on the water as it did on the shore.

Pip wanted to bake sea biscuit recipes on the dock. Long ago, sailors built a giant, heavy stone house with an entire furnace just to hold one small mixing spoon. It took all morning to set up and was far too big to carry.

Skipper squawked through his horn. 'Do not build a whole town just for one recipe!' he called. 'A container is like a tight, sealed picnic basket that holds only the exact batter and the exact spoon you need.'

Pip tucked the recipe book and the single spoon into a plain wooden box. He closed the lid tightly so nothing fell out and nothing crept in. It was light enough to lift with both paws and ready to bake immediately.

Wally floated up and offered his back. Pip set the plain box down, opened the lid, and the biscuits baked just as neatly on the water as on the dock. It worked anywhere because everything it needed lived right inside the box.

Pip wanted to bake sea biscuits at the dock. Long ago, animals built a huge, heavy shed with a whole brick stove and iron pipes just for one recipe. The giant shed took all day to build, and nobody could lift it to move it anywhere else.

Wally swam up with a clever idea. A container is like a lunchbox that holds just one recipe and the exact tools it needs to bake. Pip packed only one wooden spoon, one tin pan, and the baking card inside a single wooden crate, keeping it light and tidy.

Pip closed the lid until it snapped shut with a happy click. Instead of dragging an entire heavy building, everything the baker needed was safe inside one neat box. The recipe was ready to work anywhere because all its favorite tools were already inside.

Skipper squawked through his megaphone from his wooden post. He tested the crate on the rough wooden planks, and then he tested it across the harbor on the flat stone pier. The sealed crate opened smoothly and baked the exact same biscuits on both surfaces.

Pip wanted to bake sea-biscuits at the far dock, but the recipe needed special tools. When Pip carried just the bowl across the water, the recipe failed completely. The far dock did not have the right spoons or timers to finish the work.

Pip tried dragging a whole stone kitchen building across the harbor so everything would be included. It was far too heavy to push and blocked the entire dock. Carrying a whole giant computer just for one task was much too slow.

Wally swam up with a clever solution. 'A container wraps one job with only the exact tools it needs inside a single box,' Wally said. Pip packed the bowl, the timer, and the exact spoons together inside one plain, lightweight crate.

Skipper watched the crate land smoothly on the far dock. Pip opened the lid, and the biscuits baked instantly without missing a single spoon. The crate worked identically because everything was already packaged inside.
Skipper was looking at a small plain box. 'This box is like a special home for our app,' he said.
Pip nodded. 'When we put the app and its tools inside, it works the same on any dock.'
Wally thought back. 'Before, we built a whole computer for each app. It was heavy and slow.'
Skipper smiled. 'Now, we just pack the app and its tools into a sealed box.'
